topic.title: References Tab
topic.shortdesc: Use the References tab of the Explore side view to see the files that reference a file, and the files that it references.

body.p: The References tab (found in the Explore side view of the Personal Workspace) shows the references between one file, the file selected in the tab, and the other files of the project, as a tree. For how the tab finds the references, see .

fig.title: The References Tab Showing the Topics That Reuse a Warning

p.note: The References tab is experimental, and it is off by default. To turn it on, open your Profile page and, in the Preferences section, select Show the DITA References tab in the Explore side view. The tab is available in projects that define publications.

section.title: The Web of DITA References
section.p: The files of a DITA project reference each other. A map includes topics, a topic reuses a warning from another topic, and a topic links to other topics. Think of each file as a dot, and of each reference as an arrow from the file that holds the reference to the file that it points to. Together, the dots and the arrows make a web. The tab shows the part of the web around one file.
Besides files, an arrow can also point to a key, to an alias or to a web address. For example:

li.p: The replacing-a-failed-disk.dita topic links to the raid-levels key, and a map defines the key as raid-levels.dita. The key is a dot of its own, between the two files. The map that defines the key also has an arrow to it.

The admin-guide.ditamap map includes warnings.dita with copy-to="warnings-admin.dita", so the publication gets a copy of the topic under a new name. The warnings-admin.dita alias is a dot that has a reference to the topic that it copies: warnings.dita.
The connecting-power.dita topic links to the web page.

section.p: The rest of the manual usually talks about files as having references between them. But most of the time, the same conclusion applies to keys, aliases and web addresses.

section.title: Opening the Tab
section.p: You can open the tab from these places:

dlentry.dd: Click the References tab icon. The tab starts on the root map of the active publication.
Choose Show references from the menu of a file.
Right-click inside an element and choose Show References. The tab highlights the references to the element at the caret, or to its closest ancestor that has an ID.
Choose Show References from the context menu of an element in the tree editor.

section.p: Each of these selects the file in the tab and shows it in the Referenced by direction.

dlentry.dd: Move through the files that you selected in the tab.
Reads the files of the workspace again. The tab does not follow your edits, so click it after you change files.
Opens the selected file in the editor. When the selected file is a web address, the button is Open URL and opens the address in a new browser tab.

dlentry.dt: Use the context publication as scope
dlentry.dd: Limits the tab to the files that the context publication includes. The tab then resolves keys and applies profiling as the publication does. Click it again to return to the whole project. The browser remembers your choice.

section.title: Choosing a File
section.p: The field under the toolbar names the selected file. To select another file, click the field and type part of a file name or a path. Separate several words with spaces: a file has to match all of them. Files whose names start with the text come first, then files whose names or paths contain it. With nothing typed, the list shows the most referenced files first.

Each file in the list shows how many references it has, for example 3 in · 2 out. The tabs above the list filter it by kind, and show how many files of each kind there are: All, Keys, Topics, Aliases, Maps, Resources, URLs, DITAVAL, and Problems. A tab appears only when the project has files of its kind. Problems lists the files that are referenced but do not exist or cannot be read, and the keys that no map defines.

section.title: Direction
section.p: The two buttons under the field choose what the tree shows:

ul.li: Referenced by - The files that reference the selected file.
References - The files that the selected file references.

section.p: A file that only the project file references, such as a root map, starts on References. Every other file starts on Referenced by.

section.title: Reading the Tree
section.p: Each item of the tree is a file, or a key, an alias or a web address (see ). Expand a file to see the next level in the same direction. Hover over a file to see its full path.

ul.li: Files show the icon of their type. Keys and aliases show a key icon, and web addresses a link icon.
A red error icon marks a file that does not exist or that cannot be read.
[def] marks the maps that define a key. They come first.
[alias] marks a copy of a topic made with the copy-to attribute.
[source] is the opposite relation of the [alias].
When other files reference two or more elements of the selected file, the Referenced by files are grouped by element, under Element id="..." or Root element.
A loop icon marks a file that is already shown above in the same branch of the tree. It does not expand, so the tree cannot run in circles.

section.p: The files are sorted by kind: keys, topics, aliases, maps, resources, web addresses, DITAVAL files, then the missing and unreadable files. Files of the same kind keep the order of the references in the document.

section.title: Several References Between Two Files
section.p: When a file references another one more than once, e.g. , the tree shows the number of references next to the file. Click the number to list them. Each reference shows its kind, and the tooltip says on which line of which file it is.

dlentry.dd: Opens the referencing file in the editor, with the caret in the element that holds the reference. When there is no reference to show, the click opens the file itself. A file that the editor cannot open, such as a key, becomes the selected file instead. Clicking an element group opens the selected file at that element.
Available in the menu of a file. Opens the file in the editor, or the web address in a new browser tab.
Available in the menu of a file. Selects that file in the tab. Use Back to return.
